projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Edward W. Weiss was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: March 18, 2010 This is the oral history of WWII Veteran Edward W. Weiss. Mr. Weiss served in the U.S. Army with the 228th Signal Operations Company. He served in the Pacific Theater and his highest rank was Staff Sergeant. Ed was a prisoner of war. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Weiss's home in Erie, Pennsylvania, on May 1, 2005. World War II Veteran and former POW Dick Francese (ph) was also present. Ed was 83 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why don't you tell me a little bit about where you grew up.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Where I grew up? I grew up in many areas of the country.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: I was orphaned when I was four years old. My mother died. And from that time on it was from one place to another --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: -- Texas, Florida, all along the east coast. Essentially I spent most of my time in Florida. Various areas of Florida, from the north to south, wherever my father went, that's where I went.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: So I can't say that I grew up in any one part of the country.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: But when I enlisted in the Army, I was living in just north of Jacksonville, Florida. But I had come up to New York to stay at my uncle's house and finish school, and I enlisted from that New York -- from New York City.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any particular reason why you decided to enlist in the Army?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Yes, various reasons. As you know in '39 we were just coming out of the depression. I just gotten out of high school and it was -- only the wealthy went to college. So it was impossible for -- for me to get into a college or university. And I had no skills to offer to -- for employment. And after working in a grocery store shuffling groceries for $10 a week, six days a week, I decided that I needed to do something. The Army seemed like the opportunity for me to learn something. I had no skills to offer. So I felt that the Army would offer me something, some training that I could use. So that's the reason I enlisted --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. What did you say about May of '39?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: That was prior to the -- to Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: The European War was going on but that -- that was something I wasn't too tuned into, you know. It was over there and I was over here, and how much concern does a 17 year old have, you know --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What can you tell me about your basic training?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Basic training was minimal. I went to Fort Slocum, New York. There they offered a test to see if you had any aptitudes. I passed a test for signal school, went to Fort Monmouth New Jersey, to signal school and I was there for probably a good three months. Brought us up to 1940. So I got through that and then I was assigned. You didn't have much choice as to where you would go. I was assigned to the Philippines, which was all right with me. I was young. I didn't -- I wasn't too concerned about that. I know there was some places I didn't want to go. You know, Scuttlebutts said, "well, Hawaii was the number one place, Philippines was the second best, Panama was the pits and Puerto Rico was in the same category". So when they told me I was going to the Philippines that suited me fine. I had no idea where it was but I knew it was out there somewhere. So after I graduated from signal school I -- I was transported to the west coast and then out to the Philippines. I arrived there about one year later. It was -- it would have been May, 1940 -- May 20, 1940. And of course, at that time there wasn't much activity out there in the way of American presence. I think we only had, if I remember correctly, probably less than 5,000 U.S. garrison troops. That's what we basically did. We were just a presence there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your job, specifically, with the outfit?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Well, I was a high -- high speed Morse Code radio operator. So -- and I got into a little bit of cryptology, things like that. And my assignment there was to the Headquarters of the Philippine Department, which is what it was called then. And essentially all we did was go to work each day, eight, ten hours a day. I think it was every day and we handled all the communications that evolved from that command back to the states. All that -- that's the way they did it then. It was all done by radio.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: And that essentially is what -- what I did. And then eventually I was with -- at that time it was called the 10th Signal Service Company. And of course Dick was there too but he was in another section. DICK FRANCESE: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: We had different sections, radio, maintenance, telephone, landline, whatever.

sp.speaker: Dick Francese
sp.p: Yeah, wasn't I -- wasn't I doing the battery -- taking care of the batteries?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Yeah. You know pigeons. We manned a pigeon man. At that time they used -- they used pigeons.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: So, you know, we had different sections and while we saw each other we didn't work together every day. I worked with my section, Dick worked with his section, and so on and so forth.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you meet overseas or did you know each other in the states?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: I -- I was trying to recall that, Dick. I think Dick was already there.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Yeah. Dick had been there maybe a few months ahead of me.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: So he knew his way around, you know, it was -- we were a small company. The company was on only, I think at that time if I -- if I remember correctly, we probably had oh, less than 100 men.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: So we knew each other pretty well. And later on it expanded, but that was almost a couple years later before it expanded. So no, I didn't -- I -- I -- we interacted but we didn't work together. Then I went -- after being in Manila for awhile and getting a little bit tired of that place, I requested and I got assigned to Baguio, which is up north.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: In the mountains, it was a lovely place.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: And again it -- we were a small contingent there, about 10 people. And by that time I had been promoted to sergeant. So theoretically I was in charge of that thing, but it was very laid back and that was good.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Before you get to too much of that, what didn't you like about Manila?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: It -- first of all it smelled bad, okay. And it was -- it was oppressive, the heat was oppressive. I just thought, well, maybe a change would be good.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How about life in general, the Philippines, the time before the war started. What was that like for you?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: It was -- it wasn't -- it was actually very good duty. We -- we didn't do any KP which we had done in the states. They had civilian Filipinos who did that. We had a houseboy. We paid him so much per month for each service. He came in, made up the bed, took care of all our laundry, shined our shoes, all that good stuff. So actually all we had to do was come and go as long as we did our duty. We didn't have any formations. My section didn't have any formations like you see in the Army, fall out, roll call. Because it was -- it was a 24-hour day job. So some of us worked from -- until midnight and some of us worked from midnight to 'till daybreak. So we were excused from formations. So it was very well laid back. On our off time we can do what we wanted to. But I just felt there was something more to the Philippines than Manila. And that going the assignment to Baguio, and I had heard a lot about it, and it seemed like a desirable thing. So I bid on it and I was sent up there and I was in Baguio and thoroughly enjoyed it until just about -- I'm trying to think here -- about July or August of 1941. I was up there about a year and it was great. When I was off duty, put on your civilian clothes, which we were allowed to do, and go shoot pool somewhere in a hotel, or go downtown and visit around and very nice place. So when I got back to Manila which would have been -- and that was one thing I reflected on and I may have made a mistake, and I may not have. Who knows. I requested reassignment back to Manila because I felt I was missing a lot of opportunities that weren't available to me. These different programs were coming out that I wasn't aware of until it was too late, which I would have liked to become involved in further training, higher training, different -- different kinds of training and basically it in -- included a trip back to the states to take this training. One of them was the Flying -- Flying Sergeant's Program, and I applied for that. But it didn't work out because the war came along. So, anyway, I went back to Manila figuring, well, I'm getting close to my -- end of my tour over here. So I'll end up down there, and I did. I got back to Manila -- I'm trying to think it was about -- I would say somewhere about August or so of 1941. So I went back to Manila. Well, things hadn't got any better down there. By that time they had built the -- the port area barracks.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: So we eventually got over there. But before we got over there, we were housed in Fort Santiago down in the dungeons, and that was the pits. I mean we had bunks down there but it was no -- there was water, and there was a toilet and things like that. But in order to eat we had to go to another area to get our rations. So I didn't like that very much. But I figured I only had a few more months so I could put up with it. And it hadn't changed that much. It got a little busier then it was before I left, as far as activities were concerned and things like that. Well, I was there until, let's see, about -- I worked at Fort Santiago after I returned from Baguio until -- I think it was around late October of '41 when two of my friends, and Dick knows them, Schumalusky (ph) and Rarick (ph) --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: -- and myself, we were called in to go on some kind of an assignment. And after we were interviewed by the Chief Signal Officer -- he didn't tell us where we were going but we were going. So that was an adventure I was looking forward to. And it turned out that we were assigned to this ship transport, sea transport ship that the Army had leased. There was a shortage of -- of ships, as you probably could visualize if you knew what led up to -- up to the war. So they had leased various ships from where ever they could and this was one was -- was a very, very nice ship and everything like that. And so about, I would say, late October or early November we left Manila. Still didn't know where we were going, but it was an adventure. And I thought, "hey, that would be great." It turns out that we were going to Australia and we had some supplies on board. Not a great deal but some. And we had a few military personnel that we dropped off on the way in the southern islands, and we went down to Australia, Darwin. I thought, "hey, this is great. I'm going to get to see what's down here." I never been there of course, heard about it, but that's all. Well, it turns out Darwin is a little bit disappointment. It's, if you knew -- know anything about Australia at that time it was the outback. I mean it was really the outback.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: But anyway we -- we got down to Australia to Darwin and we off loaded what supplies we had. And I didn't know what we were doing, what we were carrying, but the trucks that came out to pick up the supplies were -- looked to me like Australians and they were dressed that way. That was fine. As I stood there watching them and so forth, I recognized a couple of them. And I figured, hey, this -- either I'm losing my mind or is something wrong here? So I went down to where the guys were loading the trucks, and I asked this guy, I said, "don't I know you?" He says, "yeah." It turns out that these people were from the Air -- Air Corp, the Army Air Corp, and they were down there to set up preliminary bases for our people. It was a plan to bring our people over and establish a base in Darwin. And they were down there, but the reason they were wearing Australian uniforms is they didn't want anybody to know they were Americans.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: So, anyhow, that -- that gave me the clue what we were doing. And from there we -- we left. We didn't take anything on. We left and went to another part of Australia, and again we didn't take anything on. So then we went to another port in Australia, and by that time I guess they realized there was something for us to do. So they loaded some material, not a great deal again, on the ship and we went to New Guinea, Port Moresby, New Guinea. And when we got there we unloaded what we had, and we sat in Port Moresby there probably for about a week. And then by that time we're getting into December, late -- late November, December and suddenly we got a message and to -- we traveled under a false name. And we weren't allowed to use our radio except to receive, we couldn't send. So at certain times in the day we would get messages from Manila through the Navy and then that's how we were able to -- to know what was going on as far as we were concerned. But then when we got to a shore place one of the Australian's towns we had to use their equipment, not the ship's equipment. So, anyhow, we got a message there when we were in Port Moresby. It turned out to be orders to go back to Manila. So we upped the anchor and back to Manila we went. When we got back to Manila, let's see it would have been the 8th, it would have been the 9th. Now, they’re a day ahead out there. So the 7th would have been the 8th, and got back to Manila on the 9th of December. And the first time we -- the first we heard about Pearl Harbor was when we were about a day out of Manila. We always listened to KGEI --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: That's where we got the message, and then sooner or later we got messages from our own people, one way of course. So it turns out that if we were north of a certain -- I -- I forget -- north of the equator when we got the message we were to go to Manila. If we were south of the equator we would turn around and go back to Darwin. Well, as luck would have it we were about three hours north of the equator. As luck would have it, in retrospect, who knows how we -- it would have turned out otherwise. So we went on to Manila. We got back to Manila, like I said, on the 9th of December.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: And it was a mess up there. I mean dozens and dozens of ships in the harbor that had sought refuge under that same order.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: North of the equator and so forth. And, anyhow, we were there. The next day they pulled us into piers -- pier -- pier one.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Yeah, down the port area. And they started painting the ship. Painted it all battleship gray and all that stuff. And then they started to load us up with bombs. I mean they loaded us up with bombs. Well, that was going fine. But the next day, I think it would have been -- the next day the 10th of December was the first Jap raid on Manila, air raid. They already been up to Clark Field and done their job up there. But the first Jap raid on Manila Harbor -- and that's when they -- they liberated? Kabihi (ph), the naval base over there, and from where we were we could see the whole damn thing going on. And that went on for couple of hours that day. And we were over here, but they were bombing over there. So we were fortunate that they weren't after the area we were in. But they decided that we could no longer load bombs at the pier. So they moved us out off of Bataan and then they brought the bombs out on lighters and loaded. So, anyhow, by that time the Japs were looking for anything in the harbor. They came over the next day, the next day, they came and then they bombed the port area, and they kept that up off and on. But you never knew what they were after. So one day they bomb here and one day they bomb there. But anyway we got loaded up and we left and we were sent down to Mindanao. Now, the B-17s that were there at the beginning of the war, those who were lucky enough, had been sent down to Mindanao a week or so before the war broke out, and the rest of them were beat up pretty badly up in -- in Clark Field. So these bombs were to go down there so these people could do their job from that place. And again no escort, just go, you know, and we didn't -- we were that naive that we didn't think too much about it, you know. But as we went along there we -- we almost ran into a Jap convoy. And fortunately we got the message that they were there and we were able to take evasive action, get away. Well, anyway, we got down to Mindanao, unloaded the bombs, and then went back to Manila. And I don't say we unloaded the bombs, the people who were down there from that B-17 group came down and unloaded the bombs. We were thankful to get rid of them because believe me from -- from what I -- I have seen, what I saw thereafter, if we had been -- anything would have set that thing off, you know, and we'd -- I wouldn't be here today to talk about it. But that's the way it was. You went, you know, and things were -- had gone from worse to worse to bad. And our job then from that day on -- and I don't know when we got back there probably was just about a week after we left, early, still early December, about mid-December. We got back there and then our job was to pull people and supplies out of Manila to Corregidor and we -- we first we went in there in the daytime to do that. And whatever was there we took. We evacuated the nurses that were in Sternberg.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: We evacuated anybody who showed up. Come on we'll take you out there, and we took some supplies out and not a great deal, but whatever was there we -- we put on and we go up. Well, after awhile the Japanese paid a lot of attention to the port area, where we were or where we were docked. So they decided that it was not a good idea to run in there in the daytime. So from that time on we went in at night. We stayed out at Corregidor and then as soon as it got dark we go in. And then we -- we continued to load whatever was there. Sometimes we went in and there wasn't a damn thing there and that was frustrating. So what we would do if there was anything sitting around that we thought could be useful, like we -- we came across one place where there was a -- a lot of oil, drums of oil, and didn't seem to be there for any purpose so we just loaded those up. We loaded up a jeep, we loaded up a -- the whole post exchange from Fort McKinley, cartons and cartons of cigarettes, and Aqua Velva and toothbrushes and toothpaste and junk like that. A little bit frustrating because we figured there must be something more valuable than this. But anyway we took what we could and then the last time we were in there in the daytime was the day before Christmas. And we came in there not knowing what we were going to do. It turns out that we were going to take MacArthur and his family and whoever else was in his -- in his group there out to Corregidor. He was leaving Manila. That made sense to get out of there. So we picked up what I thought was -- I don't know the origin of it, but we picked up probably several hundred gold bars, weighed probably about 15, 20 pounds apiece and we loaded them on. And we took MacArthur and his wife and his kid and his retinue there and his servants and a couple other people and took them out to Corregidor. That would have been the 24th of December. And we took them out there and he disembarked and he established his headquarters on Corregidor.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You didn't get too close to MacArthur to --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Yeah. Well, he didn't talk to me. I talked to him but he didn't talk to me. That's the way he was.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did you say to him?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: I -- he -- I showed him where he was supposed -- to his cabin.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: I came -- he came up the stairs there. I was on duty. He didn't seem to know which way to go. So I said, "General follow me" and I took him back to the -- the number one quarters that we had which was on the sundeck and he said, "thank you" and that was the end of that. And I did see him after that on Corregidor a couple of times, but he didn't know me but of course, I knew him. But he wasn't -- he wasn't one to converse with you. But, anyhow, we got him out there okay. But from that point on, from 25th of December until the 1st of January, we made those runs in at night and take out whatever we could. And then on the 1st of - 1st of January that was the end of that because the Japanese was coming in and we were out of there. And it wasn't an easy job, believe me. The reason we stopped going in there in daytime because every time we come in we get bombed and that was a terrible experience to have those guys trying to kill you. And you were hopeless ‘cause there wasn't anything, or helpless.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Because there wasn't anything you can do. And fortunately we -- we -- we escaped. And we were caught a couple times at the pier on those daylight runs, but fortunately they missed and we only lost two people in those raids that were unfortunate enough to get killed by shrapnel and -- and it was -- it was a pretty bad experience.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How big -- how big was the crew on this ship?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: We had a Filipino crew with American staff, you know, in the essential duties. How big a crew did we have? We probably had about oh, I'd say, 50 --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: -- very good, very competent people. But the funny part about it was, and Dick can back this up, the more bombing we had the smaller the crew became.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: And I don't look, in retrospect, I don't blame them, you know, who wants to go through this if you don't have to. We didn't have a choice but they had a choice. So from time to time we lost a few members, few members, few members. But, anyhow, after we got back out to Corregidor on New Year’s Day of '42 and offloaded whatever we had, and we took some wounded out there, and we took various -- any -- anybody who showed up. If you could walk, crawl or whatever, you wanted to get on because by that time Manila was supposed to be an open city. So we went out to Corregidor and we hung out there for a day or so and the bombings came and we -- and we got beat up pretty bad. We didn't get hit but we sure got scared, near misses and so forth and so forth. I got trapped on Corregidor a couple of times when they were trying to sink the thing. And I'll tell you, Melinda Tunnel and places like that, the Powerhouse it -- it was not a very good place to be. So then they decided they'd move the ship over to the Bataan side and just have it sit over there, figuring that they'll have something for us to do. Well, they moved us over right opposite Corregidor there, just near the southern tip of Bataan and we anchored. And we sat there from about the -- probably 5th, 6th, 10th of January until mid-February, just sat there. And we go over to Corregidor once in awhile and have lunch and find out what they wanted us to do. They still had nothing for us to do. But anyway the war was getting worse, our particular area was getting worse and worse of course, on Bataan there. But anyway about the 15th of February we were attacked twice by Japs, Jap's planes. But they didn't hit us again. So we were beginning to feel pretty confident, and that they couldn't hit us. So, anyhow, about the middle of February they told us we were going -- going on a mission. We didn't know what it was again. Turns out we were evacuating the Philippine Government who were out on Corregidor and taking them down to one of the southern islands that the Japanese had not held. The idea there, I guess, at least what we were told was that it could establish some sort of a Government presence in those islands down there, which would have been Mindanao, Negros and Cebu and Panay and places like that. And Quezon was part of the plan. He was then the President of the Philippines. But he wouldn't get on the ship. So they took him out by submarine and we rendezvoused with the submarine and on one of the southern islands there. And again we -- we hid in the day and ran out at night. And -- and looking back at it we didn't have a Chinaman's chance of getting were we were supposed to go. But we lucked out and we managed to get down to -- we got Quezon and his people off the ship. He -- he was -- he was scared to death on that -- to be on that ship. He did come on board but he made us take him off. So he went on shore and he went on his own way. And we went on down to Cebu and we loaded up with supplies. They had been bringing a limited amount of food and medicines and some ammunition up from Australia by sub. And they went into Cebu, which was central to the whole Filipino Archipelago and offloaded there. And then they were trying to run it from there back up to Corregidor. So we loaded up, really loaded up with that kind of material and again we started north. And the bad part, well, it turns out it wasn't bad -- I guess in a way it was. It was a good omen. We had probably several hundred five gallon tins of gasoline sitting on the front deck on the hatch covers and it was okay, you know, hey, we carried bombs so this wasn't too bad. Anyway we -- we ran at night and hid in the day. Well, we were probably three or four hours away from Corregidor on our last leg anchored in this bay off of Mindoro when two Jap planes came. Well, you know, we had nothing. So, anyway, they decided they'd -- that we didn't belong there and they proceeded to bomb us, dive bombers they were. Well, again they missed. They came very close but they missed. They didn't hit the ship itself. They hit the lifeboats which were hanging over the side.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: They went right down through the lifeboats and that was okay. And meanwhile, the CO said -- well, I said to him, "do you want the people in Manila to know what's" -- not Manila -- "Corregidor what's going on." He said, "yeah." So at that time we had code books, but we didn't have time to code. So we just said in plain language full -- fully knowing that the Japanese Navy was out there listening --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: -- somewhere, and if not these two guys who were trying to do us in would tell their own people and they'd know we were there. So we sent a message up to Corregidor there that we worked with the Navy telling them what our predicament was and asked them for help. Well, you know, there wasn't any. There wasn't any. So the Japs proceeded to beat up the ship and they strafed us and gave us a bad time there for about half an hour. And on one of their last -- one of their last strafing runs they hit -- they hit the tins of gas and they started to burn. And of course, the more they burned the more fuel started leaking. Gasoline started leaking down into the lower decks and so on and so forth. So by that time it was time to get out of there. So the captain said, "hey, you got to get out of here." So we -- we left, and we only had one lifeboat. By that time we were down to about 20 crew members. So some of them had got off on Cebu, they weren't about to go back up again. But they had enough to run the ship. And we got into a -- a -- there was one lifeboat that wasn't strafed. That had -- did not get holes -- did not have holes in it. The rest of them were pretty well beat up. So I destroyed the code books and things like that, that was part of my job. And I got into the second lifeboat and we were probably about 300 yards off shore. And the first one had already left. The second one which I got in got about 10 yards away from the ship, which was burning pretty good and capsized because it was holed and the water was coming in and we couldn't keep it out. So here we are about a half dozen of us floating around in the water there, and we yelled and got the attention of the first lifeboat that came back and got us, and we made it to shore. So all of us who evacuated the ship made it to the beach and of course, we scattered because we knew they'd come back, which they did, the airplanes. And just sat in the jungle there watching the ship burn. Well, it wasn't very long before a Jap cruiser came around to see what was going on. Apparently, he got word somehow. It wasn't very difficult because we had to send everything in our distress message in the clear, including where we were. There was no point in sending a distress message asking for help if we couldn't tell them where we were. And that's another -- another weakness in that whole system. Is we moved on our own and, yes, they knew we left Cebu but where we were along the way? They didn't know until we showed up at Corregidor. So, anyhow, we told them where we were and of course, that told the Japs too. Well, pretty soon the Jap cruiser came around the head of the bay and followed by two destroyers. And the -- the airplanes are doing their thing up there and they continued to strafe that thing even if it was burning. I don't know what they saw. But, anyhow, by that time we figured we better get out of this locality here. So we -- we just went further back in the jungle and that -- they sat there for that night. This was in the morning about 8 o'clock in the morning. It been about the 26th, 27th of February. They sat there all night long anchored, watching the ship burn, and we sat there watching them watch the ship burn. So there wasn't much we could do. The next day an aircraft circled around strafed a little bit then went back -- back to wherever they came from. But the cruiser and the two destroyers were there until the next day and then they left. By that time the ship was a total wreck and it had settled down into the -- into the bay and so forth. It was up, about half of it was up above the water. So now we figured, okay, we got to get out of this area entirely. So we went -- we knew there was a village. We had seen that there was a village there probably five, six, seven miles away further in. So we went down there and sure enough those who had gone elsewhere, we scattered, had all managed to get together in that village. And we had one -- one man that was wounded. One of the ship's officers got wounded in the attack but he wasn't too bad. But, anyhow, we decided well, we better get out of here because the Japanese were on the other side of the island. And we figured they'd come over on this side especially since we were there. Well, the ship had been there. So they decided we better get out of there. And the way it was planned out was that we would go to the southern end of the island were the Japs weren't, and then try to make our way back to Cebu, from island to island. And we got -- we got some help from the local villagers there. And they got some Philippine donkeys, horses, mules, you know, what those things are. About that big, right? And we sat on one of them and we walked down with a couple of guys. We went down through the -- the whole length of the island on those horses. And then when they couldn't go any further -- because there was only trails on that side, no roads, just trails -- couldn't go any further we got on a -- on a native vanka and went the rest of the way. Anyway we ended up down at the southern end of the island and from there we were -- hope to get a sailboat to go to the next island and then on back to Cebu. Well, talk about luck or un -- not being lucky. The next -- the next morning, the last day of the trip we were in the vanka paddling down -- paddling down the coast, and low and behold as soon as it got light, there sits that Jap cruiser or a Jap cruiser. He's hiding behind an island. There's an island just off shore. He's hiding behind an island. I mean he's -- he's as close as from here to the road from us.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: You know, we were scared, really scared. But it was just dark enough and we just paddled like hell to the beach, and scrambled into the -- into the jungle. Why they didn't see us, I have no idea. We could see them. We could see the -- didn't see any people but, you know, a lot of ships they're pumping water over the side and they're doing this and that and everything like that. We could see all that very clearly but, anyway, we were lucky there that they -- he didn't -- he didn't -- thought we were someone else or didn't pay any attention or didn't see us at all. But I'm pretty sure it was the same cruiser that had been up in the north end of the island there. So, anyhow, after awhile there we just stayed in the jungle there. He left about noon and we went on our way from that point on. And we got down to San Jose, which is the furthest down on the island there. And we found out there was an American contingent down there, back inland just a little bit. So we felt that was great. So we went back in there to see who they were. Well, it turns out these people were down there as an auxiliary field. There was probably about 50 men down there. As they came down from Bataan and they would to man this field in -- in as an emergency field. I say field, it was nothing but a grass strip. But, anyhow, we were able -- they had a radio. We were able to tell our people, whoever was interested, that that's where we were and where we were going. It turns out these guys had just come out from the states. Hadn't been out there for a month when they sent them down there. They had a -- they had a squadron of -- as I understand it -- they were dive bombers, but the dive bombers where on a ship enroute. But the guys were already there in the Philippines. Their planes were diverted to Australia when the war started. So they had no planes. So they were to service anybody that came along, any planes that we had that came along, and that we had left, and we didn't have very many left. So, anyhow, they were from Savannah, Georgia. I'll never forget that. And they had -- there's another story connected with those -- those people, what happened to them afterward. But, anyhow, we did get a sailboat. Had to pay a guy. Fortunately the Commanding Officer of the ship happened to have cash money, which he salvaged when we went down. He had to pay one of these local sailors 500 bucks to take us from where we were to the next friendly island, and he did that. Again that night we sailed and the next day we sailed. And finally we got to this other island which was not yet occupied by the Japanese, and from there we were able to get normal transportation. Things were pretty normal down there back to Cebu and we were in Cebu, let's see, that would have put us back there about late March. Took us about a -- took us about a month to get back there and meanwhile, the natives that we met along the way feed us and took care of us so that -- that ensured our success, otherwise, we couldn't have done it on our own. But we got back to Cebu there. And we had a fairly large -- I say fairly large -- probably 100 U.S. personnel. Navy, Army there, mostly in the supply business from those subs that were bringing stuff up, transporting and so forth. So we were there until well, let's see Corregidor, fell what 10 -- no. Bataan fell what 10 -- 10?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Yeah, about -- about a month later, not quite a month later. Well, anyway, we were there until Bataan fell.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Now, the reason I remember that, is because that's the same day the Japs decided they wanted to take that island where the supply base was. So again no -- no defense relied upon on the Philippine troops, which who the hell knows where they were. They weren't there, anyhow. And the Japs came down with their convoy. And I just sat here like I'm sitting here talking to you only a little further away of course, and I could see the whole operation. They just cruised right on up there, took their time, pulled up to the pier and got off. So we went back into the hills, into the mountains that overlooked -- overlooked the harbor there. And we wandered around back up in there for probably a good two weeks and then we decided that well, we didn't decide -- everything pointed to getting out of there. There was no hope. We couldn't find any command. Couldn't find any command at all. And we finally ended up finding a supply depot they had up in the hills there. And they had a colonel up there who was from the supply part of the military and he says, "look this isn't going to last," toward that effect. "Can you help take, lead a group of -- of Corregidors," whatever they called them porters "carry their food back up in the hills a little further." We said, "sure." So, anyhow, we did that. We took -- took as much as we could up and back up in the hills. END OF DISC ONE; BEGIN DISC TWO And we still felt we had to get out of there. From what we could see there was -- it was going to be a matter of being on the run all the time. So we got -- made contact with some natives, arranged to get a vanka again.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: It's like a canoe with an outrigger to keep -- keep it from tip -- tipping --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: -- over. And, anyhow, we -- we managed to go from that island, which was the island of Cebu over to the island of Negros, which had not yet been occupied by the Japanese. So we were over there for a while, probably a week, and we had nothing with us of course. And we met -- met some American civilians there who got us some clothing, food, gave us some money and things like that. And there was no -- there was a very limited American military presence there. It was way up on the northern part of the island and we knew that -- that wasn't going to work either because the Japanese could go where ever they wanted to go when they wanted to go. So we hung around there for a little bit. Then it was decided that -- we ran into some missionaries who were going back up into the hills. They took -- took one of our guys with them to run -- to run a radio they had up there. That was Schumalusky.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: He went up there with them. He could only accommodate one -- one of us. So that left three of us yet on our own. So the missionary man suggested that we go around to the other side of the island where there were no roads, again. And that's where we wanted to be, where there were no roads, because the Japanese always stayed on the roads, and see what we could do from there. We wanted to go to Mindanao, is where we wanted to go. Again the Japanese only had certain parts of Mindanao. But Mindanao is a big island. We felt if we get down there we would be all right. But we couldn't get to Mindanao because the Japanese were patrolling between Mindanao and the northern part of the Philippines. So, anyhow, we went around to the other side of the island and we were there probably about two weeks again. And we met a missionary there and he said, "look I'm back up in the hills here. If you guys want to come with me, well, come on. I could use your help." So we figured well, for a time being that's a good thing to do. So we went back up in the hills with him and his wife -- his wife and two kids, two young children. So he helped us and we helped him. We went back up in the hills there. While we were there we came across a sailboat. But it was -- it was too big for the three of us to handle. We couldn't handle it. So we couldn't go anywhere. So we went back up in the hills there. We were probably up there about a month and we built a house and we started the garden and all that good stuff. We were up there and then we got a message. A Filipino came up with a message that there was some other Americans on that island that were interested in helping us. They knew about the ship -- sailboat, interested in helping us to sail to Australia. So now we had enough people. So reluctantly, I mean, I say reluctantly -- we left the missionary and his family up there but we were glad to get out of there. The jungle is a terrible place to have to hang out. Not -- not -- we're just not used to it, living in the jungle. So, anyhow, we went down to the coast there. These other Americans came up, took a look at the sailboat, said, "yeah, we can -- we can get this organized." They were Navy, mostly Navy people, supply again who had been on Cebu and made their way over there. So we spent about a good week getting that sailboat organized, gathering up food, gathering this and that. We got help from the people who were there. And we got water, enough water we thought, to carry us. We got -- we figured we had about 30 days worth of water and 30 days worth of food and we had enough manpower. That was -- I say a sailboat, it's not a sailboat as we look at it -- it was more like a schooner, a small schooner, and had been used to transport lumber from -- there was a lumber mill there. So it worked -- it worked out. So none of us knew much about sailing except we knew we wanted to go south. If you put the sails up, the wind would blow, we'd get there.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: But it wasn't that simple. But we -- we learned as we went along. But it turns out that the wind was against us. So we had to go with the -- do a lot of tacking -- what they call and you go that way and that way. Maybe 100 miles to go 10 miles further south but, anyhow we -- we cruised along there and we learned a lot as we went along. It was quite an adventure. And we got down to Mindanao. But by the time we got down to Mindanao, the Japs were pretty well occupying most of the major areas. (phone ringing) -- But, anyway, where were we?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Yeah. Got down to Mindanao there and by that time the Japanese has exercised more control over the island. So we figured well -- and he -- we talked to some natives there and they said the Japanese were all over the place. And the Americans who were on Mindanao were in prison camps and they were being treated pretty badly and so forth. And so we figured, hey, there's nothing here for us. And so we decided to continue on south and which we did. We -- we continued on south and we got down, probably by this time, we been away probably 40 days, 35, 40 days since the time we left, originally. And we got about oh, I would say, halfway to Australia in distance. We're talking about 1500, 1700 miles and we traveled a lot more than that because of the tacking routine. But we got down there and now we -- we ran out of charts. The only thing we had was the National Geographic Map and that was fine but it didn't show everything, you know. It's -- it's just like getting a map of Lake Erie off -- out of an atlas as opposed to getting a chart. So we really didn't know where we were. I mean we knew we were south but we didn't know where. So consequently, we had to every now and then stop from where we came across and find out where we were. And that was all right in a way, but see every time you did that somebody knew where you were. And the natives -- and the natives down there had nothing else to talk about so they talked about these guys who came down in the sailboat, and eventually the word got back to the Japanese. But, anyhow, we managed to do all right until we got becalmed, no wind, no wind at all. And we must have hung out there for about a week just sitting and during that time apparently the word got to the Japanese that we were in the area. So they sent a patrol boat out and sure enough they found us. And that would have been in August 10, 1942. So we had about oh, I'd say, we left the Philippines originally about July 1st. So we’ve been out about six weeks before they caught us. During that time we ran through a lot of weather and storms. And I think we missed a typhoon and it was quite an adventure. But, anyway, they cap -- of course, they came. We had nothing. We could do nothing. We -- we had a .45 pistol and a .22-caliber rifle and they had machine guns and riflemen and -- and mortars and stuff on that thing or canon or whatever you want to call it. So, anyway, they captured us and took us to Ambon, took us further south. After a few days in between they took us further south to Ambon and -- which was a major base for the Japanese. They had taken it from the Dutch, Dutch or Australians, 600 miles north of Australia. So they took us to Ambon, put us in solitary confinement, and we were in there for 40 some odd days. After, you know, minor interrogation -- there was nothing we could tell them they didn't already know and they didn't try too hard to learn anything. We were history. They had already got over into the Solomons and they had already got all of the Dutch East Indies. They had everything just about what they wanted. So after about 40 days of that -- 40, 45 days of that solitary confinement they took us out to the prison camp. They had a prison camp.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Prison camp, Tan Tui it was called, where they had about 1,000 Australians who had been on that island to defend it from the Japanese. But like everything else there was too few and too many of them so most of them ended up in the prison camp. So they put us out there with the -- with the Australians. No, at first they put us with the Dutch. They had Dutch people there and then when they decided they were going to move some of the prisoners, including all of the Dutch and half of the Australians, they moved us over to the Australians' side of the camp and that left us with about 525 Australians and we were nine Americans total, yeah, nine. And then later on they brought five more in that they had captured trying to do the same thing. And so we were total of 14 Americans and 5 -- 500 and some odd Australians in that camp. That would have been in October of '42. And that's where we stayed until the end of the war.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: And I stayed -- that's where we labored and that's where we went through our POW experience there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, describe as much of that as you would like to describe.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Well, at first in the very beginning it wasn't too bad. It's all relative, okay. We didn't have to work. The food was different but it was adequate and all that. But it was just boring. That's the best way to put it. But we amused ourselves. I say amused ourselves, engaged in different activities. We played basketball. We played chess. I learned how to play chess. I almost learned how to play bridge and things like that. My -- my thinking then was well, I -- the war will be over soon and I can handle this until the war is over. Well, that wasn't a very good thought because it didn't turn out that way at all. It turns out that the Japanese were using that as a supply base to New Guinea and Solomon Islands and places like that. And our people became very interested in that and they began to -- to bomb it. Well, sometimes every day, sometimes once a week, sometimes once every two weeks. Well, when they decided to do that, the Japanese -- it was Navy not Army, but Navy decided that they had better start preparing for some more problems down the road. And they began building, bringing in supplies, building up, and moving supplies. I say moving supplies, they managed that warehouse downtown but they didn't want the stuff there. They wanted it out -- out in the jungle. So they get a crew of POWs to go out in the jungle, clear it, build, and move the supplies out there. That went on and on, and then there was unloading the ships that came in. You had to go down and help unload the ships. After all they had 500 people there. That's a good labor force. Coaling, that was the nastiest job of all. A lot of their ships ran on coal and we had to go down there and unload the coal, and that was a nasty job. And we unloaded barrels and barrels of oil, food supplies, and ammunition, and things of that nature, built roads, cleared the jungles. It was just a constant, constant labor. So that's -- that's essentially what -- and food got less and less and the bombing got more and more. The Japanese put a big bomb dump in the camp, either by accident or for whatever reason. It was hit, and it blew up and killed a lot of Dutch civilians who were in another camp nearby, and practically eliminated the camp. We -- we lost probably 20 men in the camp. A lot of them were wounded, of course. But from that time on everything went downhill. So that would have been 15th of Feb -- let's see, that would have been about August of -- I think -- you see we were bombed twice. I'm trying to sort out which one was which. That would have been the -- the February 15 of '43 when they bombed the camp. From that time on things got pretty bad. Food got scarce. We -- we had very limited medical supplies. It -- it just turned into a real nightmare. And it got worse and worse as the war went along. And the work continued. And it didn't matter whether it rained or not, you worked. They wanted to get the ships in and out. They wanted to get this work done. And it was very, you know, when they wanted something done, it was all manual labor. And it was very, very dangerous. And Dick would attest to that. Anything they wanted you to do it was primitive. I often said and, I say it facetiously, I don't think these people knew what a wheelbarrow was, you know, everything we moved was slings and a pole. Two men, slings and a pole.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Yeah. So that went on, and on, and on. And things went really downhill. Men -- men began to die from work, overwork, starvation, disease, and whatever. That went on. The second time we got bombed was in mid-August of 1945. When did the war end, '46?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It ended -- the war ended in '45 so --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: '45, mid -- in August of '45 we really got -- they really clobbered that place.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- this was right after or about the time the war ended?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: This would have been in August.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: They really got loaded on that place, and bombed the camp. Well, I don't say they bombed the camp, the camp was in the way.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: It got done again. So -- no excuse me -- I want to back that up, it was August '44.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: '44 when MacArthur was getting ready to move up into the Philippines --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: -- is when they bombed it. They really unloaded. That was a big base for the Japs. But they -- strictly by air they neutralized it and of course, we were there. The Japs were getting beat up but so were we, you know, anything affected them affected us. By that time food was almost non-existent. Really was bad. And we lost a lot of guys. We lost the Americans, we lost 5 from our 14. The Australians lost about 450 out of their 550 men. So it -- it was -- it was a real horror scene, and executions. The Japs were very suspicious of what anybody did. If they did that, they'd come in there wreck the camp, tear things apart, beat people up.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Well, they executed one group of men for -- the Australians, they’re a different kind of people. They figured out they could get out of the camp by crawling under the wire, which they could. Anybody -- getting out of the camp was not a problem.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Where were you going to go after you got out? It's like that guy in Japan, where was he going to go?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: And plus we had water and he had water too to put up with. You're not going to get from A to B by walking on the water. So by that time it was almost -- it was impossible to -- you get out of the camp, yes, but then what? But these Australians -- a group of these Australians figured out that they could go under the wire and go down to a native village a couple of miles away and get food and bring it back. Well, somebody down there told the Japs they were doing this. They caught them coming back into the camp one night. They rounded up everybody who had been out of the camp by having a native informant. They lined us all up and the guy went down the line said, "this guy and this guy." And out of that group they took -- they must have had about 15 of the Australians who had been out. They took about five of them who they thought -- I guess for whatever reason. I don't know what their thinking was -- took five of them away. That was the first executions for doing that. And then from then on it was a guy here who violated -- who stole a can of food or a guy here who did something or did what they thought he did or didn't or whether he did it or not, trying to escape. One or two did try to escape.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: And even though they had nowhere to go.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: And they got caught. You couldn't get off of that island without having help, and help involved people willing to risk helping you. Secondly, you needed a vanka or something to get from here to there. And then how far did you have to go before you would clear of the Japanese? You had a long way to go. So as a result they didn't get off the island. They got up in the hills but they were turned in by natives who were sympathetic to the Japanese.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: And you talk about different cultures. Well, I mean I'm not saying this because I'm -- any other reason other -- it was the Muslims who were more pro-Japanese than the other people were. And I think they figured it didn't make any difference to them rather the Japs ran the place or the Dutch ran the place or the Americans ran the place. You know, whoever was running the show that was the people they had their allegiance to. And the Japanese were there so that's the way it went. And the Japanese were pretty bad on some of those people too who didn't -- didn't agree with them. But anyway that's -- that's where we were. Until let's see, when was it? It must have been about -- we didn't know what was going on. We had no -- no idea what was going on in the world. But one day the interpreter came down, they lined us up to go to work and they said, "you don't have to go to work today. There's an -- there's an armistice. This was sometime in August, late August of '40 -- '40 --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: '45. They said that there's been an armistice and if everything works out, words to that affect, you don't have to go to work. But if it doesn't work then you're going back to work. So okay, we didn't know what to make of that because they've been deceiving us all those years. And not knowing any different we had to rely upon what -- what we were told. So the next day they lined us up again, I think it was the next day, next day or day after lined us up again. We didn't go to work. Lined us up again and said, "the war is over and you're going to go -- soon you'll be going home." I went "hey, that's great," and let it go at that. But we were still not allowed to leave the camp. Now, the reason for that was -- the reason they gave for that -- and I don't know whether -- well, probably some of us -- some of the Australians would have gone because they -- they seemed to know what was going on there. They had been there a month or so before the Japanese took the island, so they had a little knowledge of what was going on. They had met some people and they -- they knew what -- they knew their way around a little bit. The -- we were there and they wouldn't leave -- let us leave the camp and then when they were asked, "why we couldn't leave the camp." They still had guards at the gates. Why we couldn't leave, they said, "well, that the Army" -- there was some Army units in that area did not want to surrender. And they were concerned that the Army units would come over and take some revenge on us. Unbeknownst to us part of the -- the surrender deal or post surrender was that the Japanese would be responsible for the safety of all POWs they had. And the Navy took it seriously but the Army didn't. So the Army was at odds with the Navy who controlled the island really. And the -- the Navy headquarters didn't want us out roaming around where we would be subject to possible retribution from the Army units. So okay, we'll go along with that. Anyway after a series of -- of talks by some of the officers in the camp, they convinced the Japanese to -- to bring in food and supplies and medical supplies, which we had none before. Food was none and almost none and medical supplies were absolutely none. Which they did, they did bring it in. They brought in all kinds of food. They brought in medical supplies. They brought -- they put electricity in the camp. We never had it before. All that time it was dark. They did everything but let us go out of the camp. So that was fine. But then after awhile we decided -- we -- I say we -- when I say we I mean people within the camp. There was about 120 of us, then decided we -- we weren't going anywhere here, let's get out of here. So they asked the Japanese or demanded to know what the Japanese were doing about getting us off that island. Because guys were still dying even though we got more food and medical supplies and things like that. They said they had -- had to contact their headquarters in Singapore and they would contact their people in Japan and then they would decide when we were going to get off of there. So we figured that could be a long process. So we demanded a radio. And my job -- I was there as radio operator and there was -- Clyde was there. We had -- we had two radio operators. So we figured we could do something.

sp.speaker: Dick Francese
sp.p: And Schumalusky stayed with the missionaries?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: (Ed) Yeah, he stayed with the missionaries. Yeah, he stayed with the missionaries, but that's another story about --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: -- what happened to Steve but -- so they did, they gave us a radio but it didn't work. I mean it had limited range. The frequencies we knew were early on in the war and -- but we gave it a try. So that didn't work. So we told them that it wasn't working. We need something more. So they agreed and took us down to their main depot there. And they had a pretty elaborate setup --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: -- in the mountain, in the cave. They had equipment like we had, you know, big time stuff and that worked. So we communicated with our people. I -- I communicated with a base in Morotai --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: -- which was up 300 miles north of us.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: -- and we told them our predicament and that we needed to get out of there because things were bad. If we didn't all die from the sicknesses we had we were in danger of being killed by the Japanese Army guys and so on and so forth. So eventually they said, "okay, we're coming down." So they sent three Australian corvettes down to Ambon and we talked to them. As they came along and all that stuff the Japanese were very cooperative once we had done this. And they came down and they got there, I think, on the 10th of September of '45. And they -- they sent instructions down which we dutifully copied down for the Japanese and told them what they had to do. They loaded us up on -- on the trucks, took us down to the pier where the corvettes came and after some preliminary work there with the -- between the Japanese and the Australians -- they were all Australians -- they put us on these corvettes and took us back up to Morotai. We got back up to Morotai on the 12th of September of '45. So that's how that ended. And from there back to the Philippines, eventually back to the States. So that's how that worked.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, as far as the -- a couple of questions.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The guards, were they abusive in general to you?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Let me put it this way, they were pretty nasty.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Yes, they were. It depended -- some guards were not. Some guards just did their job. Some of them seemed to delight in making -- in -- you making it as miserable as they can for you, and they didn't hesitate to beat on you. They all carried -- of course, they had a rifle but they all had like a pickax handle or something of that nature. If you didn't do something that they thought you should do, they let you have it. If you weren't working fast enough, they let you have it. If they caught you doing something that you weren't supposed to do, they let you have it. Oh, they -- they wouldn't hesitate to beat -- to beat you. And some of it was pretty brutal, pretty brutal. And as I say, some of them just did their jobs. They just guarded the prisoners and others just looked for opportunities to inflict punishment. And I'll tell you, they were -- they were -- they were dogs. And we had all kinds of good names for them, you know. And every time you went out on a work party you'd always look and see who your guards were because then you'd know whether you were in for a tough day or you were going to get a routine day. So they weren't -- they weren't very -- very nice. I -- I don't know, you know, it was -- it was up to the local commander as to what form of discipline he'd put in there, even amongst his own people. And when it came to prisoners, there was no hesitation. If they thought you had done something wrong, whether you had or had not, you were going to get it.

sp.speaker: Dick Francese
sp.p: You didn't have a chance to defend yourself.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: No, first of all, we couldn't talk to them.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Right. Had to go through an interpreter, if they were to let you have an interpreter, and they didn't have too many of them. But the interpreter, if he was available, would interpret, you know. But no defense, no. You had -- there was no defense. You're a prisoner of war. That doesn't matter you had no defense. That was their attitude. And we were just like -- like I -- best way describe it, was just like slaves, period. Slaves. And that was -- that was what -- that was one thing that -- that still bothers me today. How willing they were to do these things. No reluctance at all. But yet when the war ended they claimed, "oh, I didn't really want to do that but I had to do it." And I don't know whether that was really the truth or not. From my -- from my observation of what went on out there with those people, they did it because they enjoyed to do it. That's the way it went. I don't -- I don't know. People said -- they said this before about the Baatan Death -- Death March. Dick knows more about that then I was because he was in it. I was lucky enough to escape from that. But Yamashita -- there's a lot of controversy of whether he should have been hung. Wasn't he hung, Yamashita?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: And when he didn't really have any direct -- but that again is -- is the thing, did he or didn't he?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Did Hama (ph) do what he was told to do by Yamashita. Yamashita do what he was told by the Emperor, and so on and so forth. And that's another area that bothers me a great deal, is the Emperor because he got away scot-free. Now, I understand why they did that but it's hard -- hard to accept.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Very hard to accept. That this man who they claimed had nothing, practically nothing to do with the war and all that stuff and let him get off scot-free. Now, it turns out that in the long run by keeping him there and saying we can't do anything to the Emperor, they were able to -- to gain control over the Japanese Government or Japanese islands much more easily then if they had taken him out and hung him.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: So there was some rationale to that. But to say the man was innocent of what was going on, that's not so. Every time the Japanese would take a beat on us, they'd say, "for the Emperor, for the Emperor." I got so damn sick and tired of hearing that, "for the Emperor." It's like we were fighting the war for Roosevelt. We weren't fighting the war for Roosevelt. But they were fighting the war for the Emperor.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, do you think -- I couldn't be inside of their heads obviously -- do you think a lot of that was really a motivation or was there also a lot of racism against --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: That's another area. There's a lot of areas there, right?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: First of all, they -- they were -- the Japanese soldiers were very well disciplined and very brainwashed, that the Emperor is a God. What you’re doing is for the Emperor. No matter how -- what the chain of command is, it's for the Emperor. Now, when you talk about their racism, yes, it was evident. I didn't hit on that too much in my book. But from time to time they would say to us -- say -- indicate to us, "look, you're that tall and we're this tall, and you're white and we're brown, black," whatever; they’re not all brown some of them are black. "The color of my skin and the color of your skin, I'm the boss." And the idea, whole idea, was at the few -- few lectures we got from the interpreter, from time to time was "get the white man out of that area of the world," whether he's American, England Dutch or whatever. "Get the white man out of there." Asia for the Asiatics, that was their motto. But the average soldier didn't believe that. I mean I -- he -- he -- it's the higher ups who were preaching this gospel. And that's what they told to the -- to the local population when they took over. Filipinos, Indonesians, the Chinese whoever they were, Asia for the Asians. You and I the same color of skin, so we should be running that and these Caucasians should be out of here. And they did use that ploy, absolutely. Yes, yes indeed. And they told us and, you know, we laughed. I shouldn't say we laughed because we didn't dare laugh at them. But it was humorous to us, you know, in a way but they had us. So you can't say, "well, look you’re wrong, you son of a bitch," you know, you just listened. Not to display any emotion.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: But they did bring that up from time to time, that we were white and they were, whatever. They say the yellow race, they aren't yellow they're more like a brown or light tan. As I say some of them were black even. They were the boss and we were the -- we were the peones. We were the slaves. That was their goal. Another thing too was it didn't come into play too much but it did somewhat, was their -- their religious beliefs, you know, they believed he was God and so on and so forth. That came up from time to time but you didn't dare say anything. You didn't dare act like you disagreed with them. You listened, that's all. They didn't try to convert us to their -- to their way of thinking, like the Koreans, that -- you know, the Vietnamese, and whatever reeducation stuff like that, no. They didn't try any of that. No, no. That was one thing they didn't try. At least not on me or my group, so --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: In the camp did you have any particularly close buddies that you remained -- stayed and hung around with when they ended the camp?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Well, as I say, we were 14 Americans --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: -- and the Australians. The Japanese segregated us. They segregated us without wire. They just said, "this is your hut," shed, it was more like a shed. This is where you stay and this is where the Australians stay. You're not supposed to talk to them. Well, after awhile, heck, that went down the tubes. So we -- we were on a group. We worked together as a group, the Americans and sometimes the Dutch and sometimes the Australians. We'd be mixed. But most of the time we went as a group. The -- the 14 Americans went out on a work party together and we may have had some Australians with us and we may have had some Dutch with us, but we were a group.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: You know, so we got some pretty good jobs.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Yeah. We got -- we got some of the shits they handed out there. They made us wear a red tag, piece of red cloth on our -- somewhere on our - we wore it on our pants there so that they could tell --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: -- they could tell who the Americans were. (phone ringing) Let it ring unless it bothers you. I got the answering machine on. So they made us wear that so they could tell.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: And some of the guards looked for that because then they gave us the hardest work, naturally. And you could understand that a lot of -- a lot of the problems that came about on work parties, not that they wouldn't have happened anyhow, was the fact that we couldn't understand what the Japs --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: -- were saying. And if we didn't do it he would stand and yammer -- yammer at you. You didn't know what the hell he wanted. And if you didn't respond, bang.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: So that was one of the things that contributed.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: And sometimes we would have someone who could speak English. A Jap guard who'd know enough English or an interpreter, if it was a big enough job. But usually it was by yammering and telling you to do this, do that, there's a pile over there, he'd indicate, take that pile and move it over there. Well, you get the message, right?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: But some of the things you couldn't understand what he wanted. So that often made a problem. But that -- I guess that's pretty common, you know, but a lot of the Germans of course, could speak English. So you'd know what they wanted. And many times if you had known what they wanted you could have avoided getting beaten.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: They didn't realize that. They just -- if you don't want to -- if you don't move when I tell you, I'll help you move, you know, so --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How long was it before your family found out that you were a prisoner?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: They didn't know until the end of the war.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you reported missing to them?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So they just -- one day they stopped hearing from you?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: See some -- we were not allowed to write --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: We couldn't do that. They didn't offer that. We never got any mail. We never got any Red Cross packages. We never got anything. We were just there.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: (Ed) And that was one of the dis -- disadvantages or advantages. I don't know how -- depends how you look at it, that we were there and some of us survived. Guys went to Japan they got a Red Cross package, they got cards and they didn't survive.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: (Ed) So who's to say where the balance is.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: (Ed) So we were -- we were just out of sight out of mind. Not out of mind but out of sight. So they did not know where we were our group of 14 until the end of the war.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Because we did not turn into a -- into the prison camp. And I don't know how -- how the Japanese worked that. I guess, apparently, they must have taken names, right?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Did they take names in -- in --

sp.speaker: Dick Francese
sp.p: Yeah, and my -- my mother found out that I was a prisoner. I think, it was about a year later.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Yeah, see, but you had to sign up or they took your name or something?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: And gave it to somebody, the Red Cross or somebody?

sp.speaker: Dick Francese
sp.p: No, the Japanese Government took it.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Yeah, see, where we were wasn't Japanese Government it was a bunch --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: (Ed) -- radical military, you know, and as I say, whether you lived or died depended where you were and who was the commander. Was he -- was he restricted by his proximity to -- to the Central Government or was he out in the field somewhere doing what he damned well pleased.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: And that's were a lot of trouble came in.

sp.speaker: Dick Francese
sp.p: How did they get you back to the states, fly or boat?

sp.speaker: Dick Francese
sp.p: Yes. Well, the thing is coming back from the Philippines they flew a lot from Japan. They flew a lot back but a couple of -- of planes went down.

sp.speaker: Dick Francese
sp.p: Everybody went back by boat after that.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Yeah, we came back by -- by liberty ship.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, to San Francisco so.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Trip? Well, it wasn't too bad. But I'd say it was, let's see, October, I'd say it was probably three weeks.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember what was your mood on that trip? Were you kind of thinking about all that had happened or were you trying not to think about what had happened?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Well, naturally you thought about what happened. But you were looking, I think, looking forward to what was ahead --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: -- more or less. And it just seemed like it was -- it was -- your life was going back in reverse, you know. We went out, you looked ahead to that. When you were young and naive you looked ahead to getting there. Now, you looked ahead to getting back, and of course, you wondered what was -- what was back there? What's, you know, it had been for me from the time -- I don't know about Dick there -- but from the time I left San Francisco going out to the time I got back was five years and seven months and now that's -- that's a long time.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: And lots of things have changed. And you didn't know who was back there that you knew when you left. So you sort of like -- you were like open ended.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: What's -- what's next, you know, reestablish your contacts.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: And go from there. And then what's ahead? That was another thing. Now, what? Before you had -- before when you went into the Army you had a structured life. You kind of in a Japanese camp, you had a more structured life. Now, you were not going to have a structured life. Now, what am I going to do, you know. So, anyhow, that's about it unless you got some -- as far as I -- I --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You think we covered it? As -- as much as we can?

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: I -- I think you have, yeah.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: There's a lot there that you --

sp.speaker: Dick Francese
sp.p: I think you did real well, Ed.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: -- that you don't really need or want or whatever.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, there's so much detail in the book, too.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: Yeah, but -- so that's the way it goes, you know. I'm just sorry that it had to -- I mean I -- I feel very -- I can be -- I can feel very sad.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: About how it turned out when it didn't have to turn out that way. See guys I knew, you know, when you -- when you run around the hills back there with guys, and you spend almost two months on a damn sailboat with them and go through all that stuff --

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: -- and then you're still together in that prison camp and they survived all that other stuff. Now, they died there.

sp.speaker: Edward W. Weiss
sp.p: They -- they didn't do anything. They were just trying to exist. They didn't challenge the Japanese in the camp. They did their job. But they got sick, they got starved, and stuff like that. So that -- that bothers me a lot. Why -- why these people had to -- didn't have to, but why they died under those circumstances.
